behavioral.text: Sure. The project I am proudest of is moving our billing service from one Postgres database to a sharded setup last year. We were a team of four engineers. I wrote the migration plan and built the dual write layer myself. The hard part was that a senior engineer wanted to do it as a single weekend cutover, and I thought that was too risky, because billing mistakes reach customers directly.

His view was fair. A long migration keeps two systems alive, and that costs the team for weeks. So instead of arguing, I asked for one day to put numbers on both plans. I wrote down what could fail in each, how we would notice, and how long a rollback would take. The weekend plan had no clean rollback once new writes started. Then I proposed a middle path: dual writes behind a flag for two weeks, a nightly job comparing both databases, and a cutover per customer group.

He agreed once he saw the rollback numbers, and he actually took ownership of the comparison job. In the first week it found two rounding bugs that would have hit about three hundred invoices. We finished one week later than his plan, with zero billing incidents, and we still work together closely. What I learned is to turn a disagreement into a shared list of risks early, instead of a contest of opinions.
Looking back, I was right about the rollback, but he was right that two weeks of dual writes was too long. Next time I would cap it at one week.

design.text: Before I draw anything, let me check the numbers. Sixty thousand seats, and about three million fans in the first couple of minutes, so reads are far above writes, and there are only sixty thousand successful writes in total. I assume a seat hold lasts a few minutes while the fan pays, and overselling a seat is never acceptable. Is that right?

At a high level, fans first land in a virtual waiting room that admits them at a steady rate into the purchase flow. Admitted fans read the seat map from a cache that is refreshed every second or so. When a fan picks a seat, the booking service does a conditional write in the database, from free to held with an expiry, so only one fan can ever hold a seat. Then the fan pays through the processor, and the callback marks the seat as sold.

Let me go deeper on the booking path, because that is where it can go wrong, and I want to cover consistency, payments, hot spots and bots together. The seat table is the source of truth, and every seat row has a status, an order id and a hold expiry, and the only way to take a seat is an update that says set status to held where status is free or where the hold has expired, so two fans can never both win the same seat, because the database applies that condition atomically, and the loser simply gets zero rows back and sees the seat as taken. The seat map cache can be a second or two stale, and that is fine, because showing a seat that just went is tolerable, while selling it twice is not, so the cache is never trusted for writes. For payments, every order gets an id before we call the processor, and the callback is keyed by that order id, so when the processor calls back twice, the second call finds the order already paid and does nothing, and if the payment fails or the hold expires, a sweeper releases the seat back to free, and the waiting room can admit one more fan. For the hot partition, one event is a single hot key if we shard by event, so I would shard the seat table by event and section, which spreads sixty thousand seats over many partitions, and the waiting room keeps the write rate far below what those partitions can take anyway. For bots, the waiting room is the right place to defend, with a token per account that is issued once, a limit of four tickets per account, and a check on how fast accounts move through the flow, so that bots never reach the booking service at full speed. And if the seat map service starts timing out at ten o'clock, fans in the purchase flow can still be offered best available seats in a section, which only needs the booking service, so we degrade the map, not the sale, and the waiting room slows admission until the map recovers, while the page tells fans what is happening, so they do not refresh and make it worse. On the read side, the seat map is served per section, so a phone only downloads the section the fan is looking at, and the cache pushes small updates for the seats that changed instead of the whole map every second, which keeps three million phones from hammering the read path, and it also means a fan on a weak mobile connection still gets a map that loads in a moment.

To sum up: a waiting room to meter fans, a cached seat map for reads, an atomic conditional hold in the database as the source of truth, and idempotent payment callbacks that release holds on failure.

meeting.text: Thanks for making the time. We build reminder software for mid sized clinics. Patients actually answer our reminders, so no shows drop by about a third. We work with forty clinics today, and we are raising one and a half million dollars to grow our sales team.
Revenue is sixteen thousand dollars a month, growing about fifteen percent month over month. Monthly churn is two percent, and a clinic pays back what it cost us to win in about five months.
I would like to hear from both of you. Tom, you have been quiet so far. What is your biggest concern with this round?

That is fair. Our cohorts are young, so we track churn by the month a clinic joined, and our oldest twelve clinics have not churned at all. About sixty percent of the round goes to sales, and the rest to product and support.
So my ask is simple: a partner meeting next week to discuss terms. What would you need to see before then?
